![](../../src/images/hex_complex.png){.intro_image} The fundamental data object in R is the **atomic vector**. Atomic vectors form the building block of every other data object that we will use in this course, and in fact any *single* value in R (a single number, a single word) is itself an atomic vector. An atomic vector can be described by its **class**, which tells us what kind of values it contains. All values within a single atomic vector must share the same class. In this lesson, we will explore the four classes of atomic vectors that you will encounter most often in this course. You will learn: * The difference between double numeric and integer vectors * How to work with character values, including when single quotes are (and are not) necessary * What a factor is and why the order of its levels matters * How logical values are stored and tested, including a common mistake that catches almost everyone at least once [{{< fa exclamation-triangle size=2x >}} Important!]{style="color: red;"} This lesson assumes that you have completed [Preliminary Lesson 1: R & RStudio](0.1_intro_to_r_and_rstudio.qmd){target="_blank"}. As the material covered herein will build on the content in that lesson, please do not proceed until its completion.
To get the most out of this lesson, please: * Open RStudio in a clean session; * Open a new, blank script file and save it as "lesson_0.2.R"; * Code along with the content! ## Numbers There are two kinds of number values that we will work with in this course: * **Double numeric**: For our purposes, this can be thought of as a decimal number * **Integer**: A whole number Let's create an atomic vector of numbers and assign it to the name `number_object`: ```{webr} #| autorun: true number_object <- c(1, 1, 2, 3) number_object ``` We can determine the class of the vector with the `class` function: ```{webr} class(number_object) ``` How an atomic vector is stored in your computer is known as its **type**. We use `typeof` to determine this: ```{webr} typeof(number_object) ``` Notice that numbers created with `c()` are stored as double numeric by default -- even though every value we supplied was a whole number! To generate an integer vector of adjacent whole numbers, we use the colon function (`:`), which generates a regular sequence from a starting to an ending value: ```{webr} #| autorun: true my_integers <- 1:3 class(my_integers) typeof(my_integers) ``` If we want to generate an integer vector with `c()`, we add an uppercase `L` after each value: ```{webr} class( c(1L, 1L, 2L, 3L) ) ``` We can also convert a double numeric vector to an integer vector with `as.integer`: ```{webr} class( as.integer( c(1, 1, 2, 3) ) ) ``` ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [`as.integer()` truncates, it does not round!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} `as.integer()` is only safe to use if the values that you are converting are already whole numbers. Notice what happens when we convert decimal values to integers: ```{r} as.integer( c(1.1, 2.3, 5.8) ) ``` `as.integer()` truncated (i.e., dropped) the decimal portion of each value rather than rounding to the nearest whole number. ::: Likewise, we use `as.numeric` to convert an integer vector to a double numeric vector: ```{webr} class( as.numeric(1:3) ) typeof( as.numeric(1:3) ) ``` ### Exercise ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Without assigning anything to your global environment, use `c()` to combine the numeric values 8, 13, and 21, and determine the type of the resultant object. Then, convert the values to integers and determine the type of the result again.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} ```{webr} #| edit: true #| min-lines: 5 ``` ::: ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [This editor won't auto-format your code!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} Unlike RStudio, the code editor in these practice boxes does not automatically indent your code as you type -- pressing Enter after an opening parenthesis or a pipe will not indent the next line for you the way RStudio does. Get in the habit of indenting your own code as you go here; it's good practice for when you're writing real scripts in RStudio, where our [style guide](../module_1/1.6_course_style_guide.qmd){target="_blank"} rules do apply (and are graded!). ::: ::: panel ```{r} c(8, 13, 21) %>% typeof() c(8, 13, 21) %>% as.integer() %>% typeof() ``` ::: `r fitb(c("It changed the way the values are stored", "it changed the way the values are stored"), width = 45, ignore_case = TRUE)` What did `as.integer()` change about the values in the exercise above? (Hint: it isn't how they printed.) ## Characters A **character** value is a symbol or set of symbols from a given alphabet (this may also include numbers and punctuation). When a character value is made up of more than one symbol, it is often called a **string**. Character values are always enclosed in quotation marks. The code below creates a character vector and assigns it to the name `months`: ```{webr} #| autorun: true months <- c("March", "February", "January", "January") ``` The class and type of a character vector are both `"character"`: ```{webr} class(months) typeof(months) ``` Any atomic vector can be converted to a character vector with `as.character`: ```{webr} as.character(1:5) ``` ### Single or double quotes? Single (`'hello world'`) and double (`"hello world"`) quotes can largely be used interchangeably in R. **In this course, we will always use double quotes for character values** -- this is the convention set out in our [style guide](../module_1/1.6_course_style_guide.qmd){target="_blank"} and it matches the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#character-vectors){target="_blank"}. There is exactly one situation in which you will need to reach for single quotes: when the character value itself contains a double quote. Watch what happens when we try to enclose a quoted phrase in double quotes: ```{r, error = TRUE} "Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds"" ``` R reads the second double quote as the *end* of the string, and has no idea what to do with the text that follows. We can resolve this by enclosing the entire value in single quotes instead: ```{r} 'Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds"' ``` The reverse problem occurs if a character value contains an apostrophe and is enclosed in single quotes: ```{r, error = TRUE} 'Maude's Cadillac' ``` Because our course convention is to default to double quotes, this particular problem should rarely come up -- but it is worth knowing that the fix is the same in either direction (switch to the other kind of quote) or that you can **escape** the problematic character with a backslash, which tells R to treat the following character literally: ```{r} "Maude's Cadillac" 'Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds"' "Maude said, \"to me they will always be glorious birds\"" ``` ::: mysecret {{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [So when *should* I use single quotes?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} Only when the character value contains a double quote. If you find yourself reaching for single quotes for any other reason, switch back to double quotes -- this is one of the rules that our automated style checks will flag! ::: `r torf(FALSE)` True or false: in this course, single and double quotes should be used interchangeably, based on whichever you happen to type first. ## Factors A **factor** is a value that maps character labels onto integers. A factor contains three pieces of information: * **Integer values**: An integer associated with each factor level. * **Levels**: The character values associated with each integer. * **Labels**: The character values used when the factor is printed or plotted (these may differ from the levels). Factors are useful when a character value can be grouped into one of a few categories (e.g., "juvenile" and "adult"), especially when you care about the order those categories are displayed in (e.g., "small", "medium", "large"). We create a factor with the `factor` function, supplying a character vector as the first argument: ```{webr} #| autorun: true example_factor <- factor( c("one", "one", "two", "three")) class(example_factor) typeof(example_factor) ``` Notice that the type is `"integer"` even though we typed in words! Let's have a look at the object itself: ```{webr} example_factor ``` There are four values, but they have been grouped into three levels. We can see the integers mapped to each level with `as.integer`: ```{webr} as.integer(example_factor) ``` ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Factor levels are ordered alphabetically by default!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} Notice that "one" was assigned the integer 1, "three" was assigned 2, and "two" was assigned 3 -- that's alphabetical order, not the order in which the values appeared! This can cause real problems when a factor's levels have a natural, non-alphabetical order (e.g., "low", "medium", "high"). ::: We can plot a factor to see the count of values at each level: ```{webr} plot(example_factor) ``` Given the x-axis labels, this order doesn't make a lot of sense. We can manually set the level order with the `levels` argument: ```{webr} #| autorun: true plot( factor( c("one", "one", "two", "three"), levels = c("one", "two", "three")) ) ``` We can also relabel the levels (useful for tidier plots) with the `labels` argument, supplied in the order of `levels`: ```{webr} plot( factor( c("one", "one", "two", "three"), levels = c("one", "two", "three"), labels = c("One", "Two", "Three")) ) ``` ### Exercise ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Create a factor from the values "low", "medium", and "high" (do not assign a name), then repeat with the `levels` argument set so that the values print in order from low to high.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} ```{webr} #| edit: true #| min-lines: 6 ``` ::: ::: panel ```{r} factor( c("low", "medium", "high") ) factor( c("low", "medium", "high"), levels = c("low", "medium", "high") ) ``` ::: ## Logical values R reserves the words `TRUE` and `FALSE` as **logical constants**. These are mapped to the integers 0 (`FALSE`) and 1 (`TRUE`), which means we can evaluate them numerically: ```{webr} #| autorun: true FALSE + TRUE mean( c(FALSE, TRUE)) ``` ### Logical operators We generate logical values by testing an object with a **logical operator**: | Operator | Usage | Meaning | |:--------:|:----------:|:-------------------------------------------| | `==` | `x == y` | x is equal to y | | `!=` | `x != y` | x is NOT equal to y | | `!` | `!(x)` | NOT x | | `\|` | `x \| y` | x OR y | | `&` | `x & y` | x AND y | | `%in%` | `x %in% y` | x is a set of values found within y | | `<` | `x < y` | x is less than y | | `<=` | `x <= y` | x is less than or equal to y | | `>` | `x > y` | x is greater than y | | `>=` | `x >= y` | x is greater than or equal to y | ```{webr} 3 < 4 3 > 4 2:4 == 3 ``` ::: mysecret {{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [Be careful when comparing two sets of values with `==`!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} This is one of the most common mistakes that early R users make (we will see it again, applied to data frames, in ***Lesson 1.3: R Objects***). Notice what happens when we compare two integer vectors of the same length with `==`: ```{r} 2:4 == 1:3 ``` You might expect two of these to evaluate to `TRUE` -- but `==` compares values *by position*, not by set membership. To test whether values in one vector are found *anywhere* in another, use `%in%` instead: ```{r} 2:4 %in% 1:3 ``` ::: ### Exercise ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Consider the vectors below. Use a logical test to determine which of the spring months also occur during the summer, and count how many summer months also occur during the spring.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} ```{webr} #| autorun: true #| edit: false spring <- c("March", "April", "May", "June") summer <- c("June", "July", "August", "September") ``` ```{webr} #| min-lines: 4 ``` ::: ::: panel ```{r} spring %in% summer summer %in% spring sum(summer %in% spring) ``` ::: `r longmcq(c("They test equivalence between two sets of values, regardless of position", answer = "They test equivalence between two sets of values, but only ever produce a result the length of the vector on the left-hand-side", "They can only be used to compare character vectors", "They are directionally agnostic, in the same way == is"))` Which statement best describes how `%in%` behaves? ## Reference ::: panel * **Character**: A symbol or set of symbols from a given alphabet (note: also includes numbers and punctuation). * **Class**: A blueprint that describes an object's structure. * **Double numeric vector**: An atomic numeric vector where the values are stored as decimal numbers (essentially). * **Escape character**: A backslash (`\`) placed before a character to tell R to treat that character literally rather than as part of R's syntax. * **Factor**: A value that maps character labels onto integers. * **Integer**: A whole number, or an atomic vector of data stored as whole numbers. * **Labels (of a factor)**: The character values associated with a factor level when printing or plotting. * **Levels (of a factor)**: The character values mapped to a factor's integer values. * **Logical constant**: `TRUE` or `FALSE`. * **Logical operator**: An operator used to test a logical statement (e.g., `3 > 2`). * **String**: A character value comprised of more than one symbol. * **Type**: How an object is stored in your computer. ::: ::: panel **Important!** Primitive functions as well as functions in the *base* and *graphics* packages are loaded by default when you start an R session. ::: function_table ```{r, message = FALSE, echo = FALSE} render_function_table("functions_0.2_values.csv") ``` ::: ::: ::: panel {{< include ../../src/includes/keyboard_shortcuts.qmd >}} ::: ::: panel {{< include ../../src/includes/rstudio_panes.qmd >}} :::
